entry.title: Thundering Herds: The Scalability Killer
entry.summary: Imagine it’s 3:00 AM. Your pager goes off. The dashboard shows a 100% CPU spike on your primary database, followed by a total service outage. You look at the logs and see a weird pattern: the traffic didn't actually increase, but suddenly every single request started failing at the exact same millisecond. You’ve just been trampled by the Thundering Herd. In this post, we’re going to dive into one of the most common yet misunderstood performance bottlenecks in distributed systems: what the Thundering Herd problem is, and how to use a combination of Request Collapsing and Jitter to build systems that don’t collapse under their own weight. At its core, the Thundering Herd occurs when a large number of processes are waiting for an event, but when the event happens, they all wake up at once. Ho…

entry.title: Docker solved my pain point on My Linux desktop....
entry.summary: Recently I started learning Docker and trying to understand how it actually works behind the scenes. How Docker Engine works, how containers are isolated, and why it is so useful in real development and deployment. Docker solved one of my biggest pain points. I use Linux, especially openSUSE. A few months ago, I even made a post about PostgreSQL installation issues because many packages don’t properly support openSUSE. It was frustrating. But with one Docker command, I can run PostgreSQL or almost any database without worrying about OS-level issues. That single thing made me love Docker even more. For me, learning Docker didn’t feel very difficult because I am already familiar with virtual machines. Containers feel similar to VMs, but they are much more lightweight, resource-efficient, and practical for daily development. Still learning, but honestly enjoying the process a lot.
